stories.headline: Connor Hellebuyck booed pregame in Winnipeg return as Jets go on to beat Devils
stories.summary: Although he did not play Tuesday night in his return to Winnipeg after being traded to New Jersey, goaltender Connor Hellebuyck was booed when he took the ice for the Devils' pregame warmup.
stories.body:
WINNIPEG, Manitoba -- The Jets earned an emotional 4-2 victory over the Devils on Tuesday night in goaltender Connor Hellebuyck's return to Winnipeg for the first time since his trade to New Jersey.

Although he did not play, Winnipeg fans got the chance to show Hellebuyck how they felt. Loud boos rained down from the Canada Life Centre seats when he took to the ice for the Devils' pregame warmup.

The Jets came out energized by the crowd booing and taunting Hellebuyck to express their anger and jumped to a 2-0 lead.

The victory extended Winnipeg's win streak to four games and halted New Jersey's at five games.

Jake Allen started in net and stopped 21 shots for New Jersey, and former Devils netminder Nico Daws, who was included in the Hellebuyck trade, made 19 saves for Winnipeg.

"It was loud. Warmups were crazy. The fans here are awesome," Daws said, according to NHL.com. "They care a lot about hockey here and they care a lot about the team and it's fun. It's fun to be a part of it. It makes you want to battle that extra little bit every night for them."

Dawson Mercer, also a part of the trade, opened the scoring at 7:54 when his snap shot from the faceoff circle beat Allen. Kyle Connor scored during a two-man advantage at 15:06 of the first period when he deflected Cole Perfetti's pass past Allen. Mark Scheifele also assisted, moving him into a second-place tie with Dale Hawerchuk in assists in franchise history with 550.

"[Mercer and Daws] were pretty excited about going against their old team, they were fired up," Winnipeg coach Scott Arniel said. "It wasn't just an average or ordinary game for those two. It was something where they wanted to put their best foot forward. And they both did. They both were outstanding, which is great to see."

The Devils, who trailed 2-0 after the first period, tied the score in the second period with a pair of goals 44 seconds apart. Jesper Bratt scored at 1:14 on a setup from Arseny Gritsyuk from behind the net. Jack Hughes also assisted to extend his point streak to six games.

Cody Glass tied the score at 1:58 when he deflected Johnathan Kovacevic's shot past Daws.

After Mercer gave the Jets a 3-2 lead on a power play at 11:58 of the third period, Connor sealed the outcome with an unassisted empty-net goal.

"A high-emotion game and you want to do better for [Allen] and [Hellebuyck], so it [stinks], but we have to learn from it," Glass said. "Obviously, it was a hostile environment with this crowd and almost a playoff atmosphere, so learn from it, take what we can, but don't make it become a consistent thing."

The Devils said Sunday night that Hellebuyck would not play against his former team Tuesday night, citing a decline in their expected win probability. Hellebuyck has won all five starts he has made since the trade and said he spoke with coach Sheldon Keefe and general manager Sunny Mehta about the situation.

"I'm 14 days into a new team, and they handle their business differently than I'm used to," Hellebuyck said Tuesday, speaking to reporters there for the first time since being dealt to New Jersey on Oct. 23. "When I went in there and said my piece and said I felt it was my duty to play this game and said, 'I want to play,' I had a good conversation with [Keefe and Mehta], and I left that conversation understanding where they're at."

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

stories.body:

Western Bulldogs: 42, 52, 53, 71

State of play and players to know
Essendon will be on the clock first, holding the top selection a decade on from the last time it took the number one pick to the AFL Draft. The Dons are expected to first bid on Port Adelaide-tied forward Dougie Cochrane, which will trigger a start-of-second-round compensation pick for the Bombers, Tigers and Eagles.

There are familial lines drawn throughout an exciting 2008-born cohort. Cody Walker is the son of high-flying Blue Andrew and will be headed to Princes Park. Cochrane is the son of former North Melbourne and Port Adelaide midfielder Stuart, though he isn't eligible to either team under the 100-game father-son rule. Instead, he's eligible to join the Power as part of their Next Generation Academy as an Indigenous prospect.

Top-10 riser Sam Gayfer is the nephew of 1990 premiership Pie Mick, and Koby LeCras brings goalkicking pedigree via 2018 premiership uncle Mark.

There will be up to five club-tied talents picked in the first round of the AFL Draft. But that won't necessarily result in an extended first night. Over the past five years the first round has averaged out to 25 selections accounting for father-son and academy bids, but clubs are expecting a number closer to the traditional 18 picks in the final intake of the 18-team competition.

Stricter stipulations around matching bids is at play, with clubs only able to use a maximum of two selections when matching for a club-tied prospect, meaning the selections of Port Adelaide, Carlton, Brisbane and GWS will be absorbed as early bids are matched.

We could see a record number of Indigenous talents picked in the first round. The high-water mark was four in 2005 and 2014, and all of Cochrane, Walker, Caylen Murray (Lions Academy), Toby Krasna and Jake Eime could be taken in the first round in 2026.

Thirteen of the top prospects have already been invited to Marvel Stadium on November 19.

Ethan Drever, Arki Butler and Heath Mellody are all still in contention to be the open pool No. 1 pick, with Harry Van Hattum, Gus Teixeira, Mitch Harris and Ethan Matthews (Giants Academy) rounding out the group on top of draft boards alongside Cochrane and Walker.

Murray, Gayfer, Wil Malady and Leo Steed have also received invites in a sign of club interest on night one.

Around 65 picks are expected to be taken across both nights which would surpass the 60 selections last year.

stories.headline: Ex-San Diego FC forward Cédric Bakambu files fair housing lawsuit
stories.summary: Former San Diego FC forward Cédric Bakambu has filed a housing discrimination lawsuit in federal court.
stories.body:
Former San Diego FC forward Cédric Bakambu has filed a housing discrimination lawsuit in federal court against one real estate firm, two property owners and two real estate agents, according to information contained in the filing.

The lawsuit, a copy of which has been viewed by ESPN, alleges the defendants discriminated against Bakambu and his wife, Anne-Laure Hueber, on the basis of "familial status" by denying them the opportunity rent a house because they had children who would be living with them.

According to the lawsuit, filed in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of California, the individuals and entities listed as defendants are property owners JW Wealth and Sheila Nasehi, real estate firm Compass California III and Compass agents Gillian Gillies and Bree Bornstein.

Neither Major League Soccer nor San Diego FC are named as a defendant in the lawsuit.

Bakambu and Hueber are seeking unspecified compensatory, statutory and punitive damages, as well as declaratory and injunctive relief, attorney's fees and costs under the Fair Housing Act, the California Fair Employment and Housing Act and the Unruh Civil Rights Act.

Bakambu signed with San Diego FC back on Sept. 3, and in nine matches for SDFC, he scored four goals with one assist.

In an Instagram post dated Nov. 6, Bakambu, a Congo DR international who played at last summer's World Cup, announced that he would no longer be playing for San Diego, stating, "Some decisions are beyond our control."

A request for comment from a representative for JW Wealth wasn't successful. A request for comment from Compass was also not successful.

ESPN has asked San Diego FC and the league for comment. the MLS players' association declined an ESPN request for comment.

The suit, which was filed on Monday, alleged two instances of discrimination. In the first alleged incident, Bakambu made an offer to rent a 5,679 square-foot house in San Diego, Calif. for a monthly rent of $17,500.

The filing details how Gillies, the agent representing Compass, stated that a pool barrier "would be required due to the age of the children" and asked whether Bakambu would pay an estimated $6,000 to install it if the owner approved.

Alternatives were proposed by Bakambu's broker, Sandra Shebani, including mesh covers and splash alarms.

Gillies responded: "A barrier will need to be installed."

The requirement wasn't mentioned in the property listing.

By Sept. 16, Bakambu made an updated offer that included paying a year's rent in advance, a Pool and Spa Liability Addendum, and an agreement to pay for the barrier.

According to the filing, Compass managing director Melanie Fontana later told Shebani that another applicant that met the lease requirements was under consideration, that Bakambu's offer had been received and that the owner would fund any pool safety measures.

The lawsuit goes on to state that on Sept. 18, 2026, Ms. Shebani raised the fair-housing concern directly with Kathy Mehringer, Compass's Broker of Record and Managing Director of Compliance and Risk Management.

Mehringer responded: "Melanie has explained the process. Compass is not violating any fair housing rules - why would you accuse us of doing so? That is not collaboration."

The filing states that Bakambu's offer was never accepted, and the rental listing was withdrawn from the market after his real estate agent raised fair-housing concerns with Compass management. The suit states that by tying rental conditions to the children and their ages, Bakambu and Hueber were discriminated against.

Later, Bakambu and Hueber sought to rent a 6,300 square-foot house through Compass in Rancho Santa Fe, Calif., and on Oct. 11, 2026, after viewing the property with Bornstein, offered a monthly rent of $23,500.

The filing states: "The offer and follow-up from Ms. Hueber went unanswered even after Plaintiffs observed the home being advertised for $20,000 per month by October 26, 2026."

On Nov. 6, the rental property was taken off the market.

The suit alleges that Compass and Bornstein, its listing agent for the second property, discriminated against Bakambu and Hueber by failing to consider or negotiate their offer because of familial status, and that this was in retaliation for Bakambu and Hueber raising fair-housing concerns regarding negotiations for the first property.

While this was going on, Bakambu's family was forced to remain in temporary housing at his own expense, according to the filing.

The filing reads: "Cédric and Anne allege that this sequence was not [an] ordinary rental negotiation. They were denied equal consideration because their household included five children, and Compass subjected them to further adverse treatment after they asserted their fair-housing rights.

"The consequences were concrete: lost housing opportunities, additional expenses, prolonged housing instability, disruption of efforts to arrange schooling and activities for their children, humiliation, and emotional distress."

stories.headline: Qatar, Abu Dhabi races set to go ahead as F1 rules out Imola backup plan for finale
stories.summary: Formula 1 has told Imola it will not be required to hold a season-ending race, meaning the plan to finish 2026 in Qatar and Abh Dhabi is now set in stone.
stories.body:
Formula 1 has told Imola it will not be required to hold a season-ending race, meaning the plan to finish 2026 in Qatar and Abh Dhabi is now set in stone barring unforeseen circumstances.

F1 had created a backup plan to finish the season in Italy on Dec. 6 in case hostilities resumed in the Middle East after the U.S. midterms.

The Italian circuit had started building grandstands but needed to know whether to commit to full-scale preparations.

On Tuesday, the deadline reported by ESPN last week, F1 has now let Imola know it will not be required.

It means as things stand, F1's season finishes with a triple header of races in Las Vegas on Nov. 21, Qatar on Nov. 29 and Abu Dhabi on Dec. 6.

Formula 1 has repeatedly stressed that it has been in constant communication with governments in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, while also monitoring travel advice from relevant European countries where the sport's 11 teams are based.

F1 was emboldened by the fact that MotoGP, also owned by Liberty Media, last weekend raced without issue in the Qatar circuit hosting F1 at the end of this month.

MotoGP team Yamaha pulled out of that event due to the company's global travel policy.

No F1 team has similar restrictions about travelling to the region.

The Imola news means F1 is full-speed ahead with its original schedule plan.

Sources have told ESPN that the final two races can still be scrapped if there were renewed hostilities in the Middle East.

Sources have confirmed in that instance, without Imola, that would mean the season ending with the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

- McLaren's Piastri splits from ex-F1 driver Webber's management team

- Mercedes new era of dominance? Wolff warns of fight to retain constructors'

- Verstappen's P21 to P2: Red Bull a 'disaster to drive' in São Paulo

From a sporting context, both championships are settled -- Kimi Antonelli won the drivers' championship in Mexico, while Mercedes wrapped up the constructors' in Brazil. However, the constructors' championship is how teams are allocated their prize money and plenty of other teams are fighting for positions lower down.

Sources have told ESPN that F1's commercial agreement with the teams states there must be 22 races minimum in a calendar year, although their commercial agreements with broadcasters will be satisfied at the conclusion Las Vegas' event.

The U.S. and Israeli war in Iran earlier in the year forced F1 to cancel April races in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia, although Bahrain paid to reschedule with an event at Malaysian circuit in October.

Despite the rescheduled Bahrain race, were the final two races to be cancelled, F1 would be left with 21 races for the season.

stories.headline: Wings' Paige Bueckers, Azzi Fudd talk relationship on pod
stories.summary: Azzi Fudd hosted Wings teammate Paige Bueckers on her podcast and the two discussed their relationship, Dallas' season and Fudd's recovery from knee surgery.
stories.body:
Dallas Wings teammates Azzi Fudd and Paige Bueckers, the past two WNBA No. 1 draft picks, spoke on Fudd's podcast Friday about a variety of topics, including a personal life update.

"We're not together anymore; it's been a while," Bueckers said on the "Fudd Around and Find Out" podcast. "[We] share that because everybody [was] like, 'Oh my gosh, they're teammates, how is this going to work?'"

Bueckers and Fudd, who were teammates in college at UConn, said they felt the need to address their relationship status in part because of allegations it factored into the Wings picking Fudd at No. 1 in April. Fudd was chosen over TCU guard Olivia Miles, who went on to be the Rookie of the Year for the Minnesota Lynx. Spain's Awa Fam (Seattle Storm) was taken third, followed by teammates from the 2026 champion UCLA Bruins: Lauren Betts (Washington Mystics), Gabriela Jaquez (Chicago Sky) and Kiki Rice (Toronto Tempo).

Fudd, Fam, Betts and Miles were all No. 1 at different points in ESPN's mock draft in the months before the April draft. Bueckers said her previous relationship with Fudd had no impact on Dallas' decision.

"We were not together before she got drafted," Bueckers said. "She was not drafted because she was my girlfriend. She was drafted because she deserved it. She's an amazing human, an amazing basketball player. And we're still friends, we're still cool.

"We played an entire season together; we're the utmost professionals."

Fudd averaged 13.1 points but was limited to just 30 games after an injury to her right knee led to season-ending arthroscopic surgery in August. She offered an update on her health.

"My offseason's been good," Fudd said. "Lots of rehab, lots of training, lots of on-court workouts, lots of traveling. It's been busy.

"I think there's a lot I can improve on. Especially the iso game; I feel like I'm not too comfortable with that yet. I know I'm capable of doing a little bit more. Watching someone like Paige who is able to create from anywhere ... that's great inspiration for me."

Bueckers averaged 20.9 points, 4.1 rebounds and 5.9 assists, and was named to the All-WNBA second team as Dallas reached the playoffs as the No. 7 seed.

The Wings were eliminated in the first round by the eventual champion Golden State Valkyries. Bueckers said she learned a lot from her first playoff experience and complimented Golden State.

"The Valkyries' defense, I can't explain to you how tough they are," Bueckers said. "They swarm, they send bodies, they trap you, they blitz you, they're so connected. I'm glad I got to have that experience against them to open my eyes to what the playoffs are like -- the physicality, the pressure, the environment.

"And I'm proud of our season. I hated losing; I sat and was pissed about it for like a week. I reached out to [Sue Bird] about it, what was her first playoff experience like. I didn't play as well as I wanted to. But it was my first experience, going against a really good opponent, and I was learning and growing through it all."

Fudd and Bueckers also addressed the Wings' move to the 19,000-seat American Airlines Center in downtown Dallas next season after playing at UT Arlington's College Park Center, which seats over 7,000, since the franchise relocated to Texas in 2016.

"UTA was a vibe; we had a ball, we did our thing there," Bueckers said. "But definitely excited to move into Dallas. New times."

While the change in venue will lead to more eyes on Wings games, the two players said they're hoping for less scrutiny of any on-court behavior.

Both said fans shouldn't read into interactions the two have with each other or their teammates as anything other than normal team behavior. They also said they don't stand for "hate of any kind" or "tearing people down to lift us up."

"We've seen a lot of negativity," Bueckers said. "We've had stuff sent to us, stuff sent to our family, our friends. There's been some crazy things said about us. We still support each other, we're still going to be great friends, we're still going to be great teammates. All the negative things can be put aside, and you don't need to overanalyze everything."

Fudd added with a chuckle, "Also, we don't need messages [from fans] on what the other person's doing. We've addressed everything we need to, and the rest will stay with us."

stories.headline: On the Munny: Cam's new role depends on Walsh groins
stories.summary: Cameron Munster is in a purple patch with his unlikely goalkicking heroics in this World Cup, but whether he continues in the final will depend on Reece Walsh's groins.
stories.body:
Cameron Munster is in a purple patch with his unlikely goalkicking heroics in this World Cup, but whether he continues in the final will depend on Reece Walsh's groins.

The Melbourne magician, a free agent since November 1, said his entire focus was on winning the World Cup and would not be drawn on his club future.

Sunday's final at Suncorp Stadium is expected to be a close contest with goalkicking possibly deciding the outcome, considering the Kiwis have the game's best marksman in Jamayne Isaako.

Munster has barely kicked for Melbourne in the past four years but has been nailing them like Hazem El Masri in his pomp with 11 goals from 15 shots with many of the attempts from the sideline.

He took over from Walsh in the 66-6 win over Cook Islands and continued in the 44-12 victory over Samoa in last week's semi-final.

With regular NRL goalkickers Sam Walker and Latrell Mitchell not in the starting side, the duties have fallen to Munster and he has done a great job despite admitting he does not practise.

"To be completely honest, I don't really like goalkicking," Munster grinned.

"I just do it because we've got no one in our squad doing it at the moment.

"Reece is our number one kicker, so if he feels good enough to do it on Sunday, he'll take over.

"If he pulls up a little bit lame on captain's run with his groins, I'll probably take over."

Munster had one of his best games this year in the semi-final win over Samoa where he ran the ball superbly and was a real handful.

His 18 runs was the most for any Kangaroo and throw in his 146m and three try assists it is a positive sign for the hosts.

"When I am playing my best, it is when I'm running the ball. That's the mindset and the aim for myself on Sunday," Munster said.

"The game might not be the same against New Zealand. I'm sure they've got a plan around myself and I'm sure I'll have to try and figure out a way to get around it."

Munster made his Test debut for Australia in the 2017 World Cup when he played two pool games at centre and halfback. He did not play in the 6-0 win over England in the final, but was No.6 in Australia's 30-10 triumph over Samoa in the 2022 World Cup final.

He has dared to dream about backing that up but said the process and not the outcome was on his mind as he attempts to enure the new players in the side get the satisfaction.

"I remember one of the boys, Jack Bostock, asked me the other day what it was like to win a cup," he said.

"It's something I've been very fortunate enough to be able to win, but these guys who have only just had their first World Cup, you try to give them that taste.

"You never know, four years' time, who's going to be able to be in the squad again."

Munster said in a previous interview he would delay travelling to Papua New Guinea until a later date after postponing a planned visit to talk to PNG Chiefs before November 1 that had been approved by the Storm.

Whether he will head to Port Moresby in future was not a subject he wanted to address on Wednesday.

"I am just focused on the World Cup," Munster said.

"My manager's dealing with all that sort of stuff and once the back end of this World Cup's done ... he'll sort that out, whether that's an option. If not, then it's not."

stories.headline: Braves GM emphatically shuts down Ronald Acuna trade speculation: 'We need him'
stories.summary: Braves GM Alex Anthopoulos dismissed the possibility of the team moving on from Ronald Acuna Jr., saying, "I have no idea where that stuff came from."
stories.body:
LAS VEGAS -- If there were any doubts about the Atlanta Braves' commitment to Ronald Acuna Jr., general manager Alex Anthopoulos squashed them Tuesday when asked about the trade rumors surrounding his star right fielder.

"I have no idea where that stuff came from," Anthopoulos said at the general managers meetings. "There's not even a hint of smoke to it. There's zero."

Acuna, who turns 29 next month, was hampered by injuries in 2026 for the third straight season since winning National League MVP in 2023. He batted .255/.345/.451 with 20 home runs and 21 steals on 29 attempts in 107 games during the regular season before going 3-for-24 with a .425 OPS in seven playoff games.

The dismal playoff performance prompted boos from Braves fans during the NL Division Series against the Los Angeles Dodgers. Acuna, who said fans were within their right to boo him, fought back tears after the Braves were eliminated in Game 4. Acuna later wiped any Braves-related content from his Instagram, fueling speculation of a disconnect between him and the organization.

Anthopoulos, however, emphatically dismissed the possibility of the team moving on from the five-time All-Star this winter.

"I don't know why [there's speculation]," Anthopoulos said. "Seriously. I was just talking to our guys about it. I have no clue. And normally I would just say, if there's noise it's because there's been a conversation. There have been zero conversations. And I don't mind saying that on the record. Zero. None. No phone calls. Incoming, [outgoing]. Zero.

"I think it was just somebody on his computer, in his basement, put it out there. And, normally, if there's a little smoke, right, somebody called and asked. Maybe we made a private outbound call. None of those things happened."

Acuna signed an eight-year, $100 million deal in 2019 with $17 million club options for 2027 and 2028 that quickly became one of the club-friendliest contracts in baseball. The Braves picked up his team option for 2027 immediately after the conclusion of the World Series. And, barring an unexpected development, they'll exercise his club option for 2028, too.

"He's a huge part of our club," Anthopoulos said. "We need right-handed bats. He was an integral part of our lineup, especially in the biggest games of the year in September -- excluding the postseason, of course. He shined and he was incredible. We need him. We need to add to him. Obviously, we need more than just him. But I have no idea where that stuff came from."

stories.headline: Filip Forsberg has 2 goals, Juuse Saros gets shutout in Predators' 5th straight win, 3-0 over Kings
stories.summary: — Filip Forsberg scored two goals, Juuse Saros made 30 saves in his 28th career shutout and the Nashville Predators extended their winning streak to five games with a 3-0 victory over the Los Angeles Kings on Tuesday night.
stories.body:
LOS ANGELES -- — Filip Forsberg scored two goals, Juuse Saros made 30 saves in his 28th career shutout and the Nashville Predators extended their winning streak to five games with a 3-0 victory over the Los Angeles Kings on Tuesday night.


Nils Hoglander had two assists and Adam Wilsby got an empty-net goal in the Predators' opener of a five-game West Coast road trip. Saros finished his first shutout of the season with 13 saves in the third period against the Kings' improved effort.


Anton Forsberg stopped 27 shots for the Kings, who were shut out for the first time this season. Los Angeles dropped to 2-3-0 on its seven-game homestand with back-to-back losses.


Nashville scored early in the first period when Hoglander controlled a blue-line turnover by Brian Dumoulin and eventually made a backhand pass through defenseman Cody Ceci's legs to Filip Forsberg for his sixth goal.


Filip Forsberg scored again in the second when Hoglander flipped the puck to him from the boards for an awkward shot that surprised Anton Forsberg.


After a slow offensive start to the season, Filip Forsberg has six goals in his last eight games, including two multigoal games in the past two weeks.


Wilsby's empty-netter, which came on a clearing attempt that took a fortuitous bounce off the boards, was only the third goal of his NHL career and the first since Dec. 20.


Mats Zuccarello returned to Los Angeles' lineup after a six-game injury absence.


Former Kings general manager and defenseman Rob Blake was in attendance. Blake was named the Predators' executive vice president of hockey operations in June.


Up next
Predators: At Anaheim on Wednesday night.


Kings: Host New York Islanders on Thursday night.

stories.headline: November Draft Power Rankings: ESPN's final, top 50 rankings ahead of the draft
stories.summary: It's time for ESPN's final AFL Draft Power Rankings for 2026. Jasper Chellappah has ranked his top 50 prospects for next week's draft, with all signs pointing to a deep and talented pool of prospects.
stories.body:
After eight iterations of ESPN's AFL Draft Power Rankings for 2026, the final top 50 is here.

A truly deep and talented pool of prospects has emerged across the season, with the final draft of the 18-team era filled to the brim with prospects deserving of AFL opportunities.

A total of around 65 talents will be selected, and amongst the 2008-born cohort are three mature-agers. Jake Soutar, Jack Slattery and Brady Wright should find homes in the AFL Draft as late-developing talents.

While it's a settled top 10 of the same names, there have been sliders and fallers across the top 50. Small forward George Dimer is receiving late first round interest and has the tools to excel at the next level despite his smaller frame, and Lachie Hicks has the athletic profile and work ethic to explode in a professional environment.

Debate has raged around Arki Butler's 2km time trial of 7:29, which would have been equal-slowest at the draft combine. The goalkicker remains a chance at Essendon's first, with his best 2km a minute faster completed in pre-season. Clubs won't be concerned about a power athlete's poor run first-up off a hamstring injury and he remains at No. 3 here as the best open pool prospect.

A deep crop means there are a host of unlucky names to not feature, though they remain good chances to be drafted across the night of November 19 and 20.

WA's Tom Brown provides reliability in defence and Kai Parker (Collingwood NGA) was cruelled by injury in his top-age campaign. Jordan Knapp is a proper ball magnet, Memphis Webb will have fans as a tough midfielder and Judd Burgiel boasts wheels streaming out of defence. Gus Kennedy, Jackson Watkins, Finlay Yeo, Harry Franz and Tate Hodgson are prominent names across the draft cycle that are unlucky not to feature.

A week out from the 2026 AFL Draft, this is ESPN's final top 50 Power Rankings.

Previous rankings: April | May | June | July | August | September | October | November

Other stuff to know: Draft primer and FAQs | Every club's needs | Draft order | Jasper's most recent Phantom Draft | Full combine wrap and results

1. Dougie Cochrane (Port Adelaide NGA) (previously: 1)

Central District/South Australia

FWD/MID/DEF, 195cm

For 24 months now Cochrane has been the pick 1 apparent in 2026. It's a testament to his talent that he's stuck at one despite never playing an U18 National Championships game and registering only four games this season. He has the size and aerial prowess to thrive as a key forward, the skills and athletic profile to dominate behind the ball and the ambition to move into the engine room and become a game-breaking midfielder. Cochrane is a truly unique prospect and a consensus top of the crop. Port Adelaide are the beneficiaries on draft night, but it remains to be seen what position the son of Stuey will play his best footy.

READ: Consensus top AFL draft prospect Dougie Cochrane already in rare air

2. Cody Walker (Carlton father-son) (2)

Bendigo Pioneers/Vic Country

MID, 184cm

National Championships: 3 games, 23.7 disposals, 3.7 clearances, 1.3 tackles

Walker blends natural talent with ambition and professionalism. He's an excellent stoppage player, winning his own ball and twisting out of trouble with sharp agility and a burst of acceleration. He finds exits few others can and has already looked a class above at VFL level through the midfield. Walker's decision-making and skill execution under pressure lets him down on occasion, but the son of former high-flying Blue Andrew is a top tier prospect with the upside of a future Brownlow Medallist.

READ: 'I'm a competitor': Cody Walker primed and ready for the next step

3. Arki Butler (3)

Sandringham Dragons/Vic Metro

MID/FWD, 182cm

National Championships: 3 games, 12.3 disposals, 7.0 marks, 1.7 goals

Few draft prospects have ever borne a resemblance to Butler. The powerfully-built medium forward boasts excellent hands in marking contests, craft with either foot at ground level, a violent fend off and elite burst to create separation. He's a matchwinner inside 50, exposing mismatches and stepping up when the game is on the line. Butler has had flashes of something special as a midfielder but could be too damaging up forward to ever become a permanent on-baller.

READ: 'All damage' - Arki Butler is the 2026 draft's most watchable junior footballer

4. Ethan Drever (4)

GWV Rebels/Vic Country

MID, 188cm

National Championships: 4 games, 20.0 disposals, 4.5 marks, 4.2 tackles

Drever has all the tools to become a superstar midfielder. He can use his big frame to win contested ball, but is at his best in transition where his power and top speed changes the game. The Vic Country MVP thrives with the ball in space, making it his trademark to hit the paint of 50 and kick long-running goals all season. Drever is a high-floor prospect with leadership attributes at the next level.

READ: Power to burn and a 'trademark' goal: why Drever rocketed up draft boards

5. Harry Van Hattum (5)

Northern Knights/Vic Metro

RUC/FWD, 205cm

National Championships: 4 games, 10.8 disposals, 2.5 marks, 22.0 hitouts

Van Hattum offers a package that could make him the best player to come out of his draft class. There's little doubt that he makes it as a ruckman; he offers true ruck size with a mature body and the aggression to match an opponent's physicality. What makes him a top five prospect is the traits that other rucks can't provide. Van Hattum is an excellent ball user and routinely gets involved through the midfield, plus has an extraordinary athletic profile that helps him jump all over his opposite number. He offers a glimpse into the future of the ruck position in the AFL.

READ: 'I just hate that' - Harry Van Hattum wants to end ruck disrespect

6. Heath Mellody (6)

Claremont/Western Australia

MID/DEF, 184cm

National Championships: 4 games, 28.2 disposals, 5.0 marks, 2.5 tackles

No prospect ended the season in better form than Mellody. He took out the Larke Medal at the National Championships and ended his season with strong form in the WAFL. Mellody is a natural outside midfielder with an appetite to spread and collect a lot of the ball. He's a lovely kick and bites off damaging options through the corridor and will be a complementary piece across halfback, a wing and eventually on-ball.

READ: WA prospect Heath Mellody is this year's ultimate bolter

7. Gus Teixeira (7)

Sandringham Dragons/Vic Metro

MID, 181cm

National Championships: 4 games, 17.0 disposals, 4.2 tackles, 1.8 goals

The power, composure and skill Teixeira plays with gives him a great platform to explode at the next level. He's excellent at navigating through traffic and it gives him a path to becoming an excellent midfielder, but not before he spends time up forward. Teixeira plays with flair and aggression that will hold him in good stead.

8. Mitch Harris (9)

Woodville-West Torrens/South Australia

DEF, 195cm

National Championships: 4 games, 8.8 disposals, 3.5 marks, 1.0 tackles

Harris is the full package as a key defender. He has the size to play on genuine key forwards, offers athleticism in the air to intercept and good closing speed on the lead. There's upside to his offensive game that excites clubs as well. Harris ended the year with WWT in SANFL finals to rubber stamp his top 10 credentials.

9. Sam Gayfer (8)

Northern Knights/Vic Metro

FWD, 194cm

National Championships: 4 games, 11.0 disposals, 4.2 marks, 2.5 goals

Gayfer is the top open pool key forward. A bash-and-crash type with serious courage in the air, he presents at the ball full-chested and flies at everything he can. The combine's new vertical jump record-holder can beat defenders on the lead and in packs, and if his set shot continues to improve Gayfer will be worth every bit of the top 10 price tag.

10. Ethan Matthews (Giants Academy) (10)

Giants Academy/Allies

MID, 186cm

National Championships: 2 games, 25.0 disposals, 5.0 marks, 6.0 tackles

Matthews's game is made up of a lot of natural football instinct. He's comfortable operating in stoppages with clean hands and quick decisions, and on the outside has a fluid kicking action off his preferred left that links the chains efficiently. Matthews is a ball magnet because he doesn't fumble and gets to the right spots, and will be the highest picked Giants Academy graduate since Tom Green.

11. Wil Malady (11)

Gippsland Power/Vic Country

FWD, 190cm

National Championships: 3 games, 10.7 disposals, 5.7 marks, 1.3 goals

Malady steps up on the big stage. He was the most dangerous forward in the APS grand final and Talent League grand final to finish the season, and offers a unique blend of traits. He's an excellent runner and can impact off a wing or half forward, but is at his best aerially deep in attack where he launches at the ball with strong hands. Malady hits the scoreboard in a variety of ways which will give him every chance of succeeding in the AFL.

12. Clancy Snell (12)

Gippsland Power/Vic Country

DEF, 196cm

National Championships: 4 games, 13.0 disposals, 7.0 marks, 2.5 tackles

Snell's ultra-aggressive intercepting style has seen him come undone at times, but it's also a glimpse into the upside. No one turns defence into attack like the surehanded backman, who loves to roll off his opponent and go third man up, or peel off to intercept and kickstart transition with good foot skills. He needs to hone those defensive instincts as a one-on-one defender which could see him take more time to debut than the other first round key defenders.

13. Leo Steed (13)

Swan Districts/Western Australia

MID, 176cm

National Championships: 4 games, 23.5 disposals, 3.0 marks, 4.0 tackles

Steed is the ultimate professional that gets the absolute best out of himself. He runs hard both ways, wins the ball on the inside and can use it on the outside, and has grown his game outside of the midfield to become a solid contributor ahead of the ball. Steed doesn't let his size impact how damaging he can be as a first-use on-baller..

14. Caylen Murray (Lions Academy) (14)

Lions Academy/Allies

DEF/MID, 183cm

National Championships: 24.0 disposals, 6.8 marks, 1.8 tackles

Murray offers composure and class by the bucket load. He's an assured presence out of the backline that has the foot skills to take kick ins and link play multiple times in passages. There's upside in his composure around stoppages in the future, but he looks a readymade halfback prospect for the Lions.

15. Tyson Bradley (18)

Sandringham Dragons/Vic Metro

DEF, 195cm

National Championships: 4 games, 14.5 disposals, 6.5 marks, 1.0 tackles

Vic Metro's MVP is all but assured of finding a home in the first round. Bradley plays with an edge and is resolute in not getting beaten. He's strong one-on-one and uses his agility and safe ball use to get himself out of trouble from defence. Bradley's mature body could see him play senior football early next year, and he has leadership ambitions in the future.

16. Jake Eime (15)

Central District/South Australia

DEF, 182cm

National Championships: 4 games, 20.2 disposals, 3.8 marks, 1.2 tackles

Eime has a point of difference to prospects in the first round with his blazing pace off halfback. He tucks the ball and plays with instinctual dare to break lines and continually put speed on the ball. Eime fits the modern game and will be a weapon off halfback for the club that takes him.

17. Khaled El Souki (Western Bulldogs NGA) (16)

Western Jets/Vic Metro

FWD, 174cm

National Championships: 1 game, 10.0 disposals, 5.0 tackles, 1.0 goals

El Souki is a polarising prospect. Detractors point to his athletic testing and body shape, but you only need to watch the small forward to see how he projects at the next level. El Souki is a balanced power athlete that absorbs hits with a low centre of gravity and plays through contact exceptionally well. He's a lovely kick off his preferred left and routinely hits the scoreboard as a forward-half midfielder, high half forward or deep threat.

READ: 'They'd follow me knowing I kick goals' - NGA-tied Khaled El Souki is in first-round contention

18. Jack Pickett (17)

Geelong Falcons/Vic Country

FWD, 194cm

Pickett came into the year as the best key forward in the open pool, but had his season wiped out with an ACL rupture. He's a natural ahead of the ball, timing leads and finding dangerous space before executing set shots with a repeatable action. He has safe hands and looks most at home with the ball out in front of him on the lead.

19. Kodah Edwards (21)

South Adelaide/South Australia

MID, 183cm

National Championships: 4 games, 22.0 disposals, 4.5 marks, 3.2 tackles

Edwards rips into every contest like his life depends on it, scrapping for loose balls and thriving in the heat of stoppages. He's also shown flashes of huge upside in the forward 50 where he gets to work as the ball hits the deck and can hit the scoreboard. If Edwards's ball use and decision making comes on at the next level he will prove a steal at this price.

20. Koby LeCras (19)

West Perth/Western Australia

FWD/MID, 192cm

LeCras had his season wiped out due to a partially torn ACL, but not before a best on ground three-goal performance off a wing for the ACL Academy. He can play up the field but is also a target in the forward 50 with the ability to convert opportunities from lead-ups and ground balls. He has real smarts around goals to convert half-chances.

READ: From an ACL tear to a time trial PB - Koby LeCras on building resilience in his draft year

21. Ethan Herbert (20)

North Adelaide/South Australia

RUC/FWD, 200cm

National Championships: 4 games, 15.8 disposals, 3.0 marks, 2.5 tackles

Herbert is the standout ruck in this part of the draft. He has great hands in the contest and wins a lot of his own ball as an extra midfielder, plus has some chops as a forward where he can use his frame and hands to advantage. He should build into being a genuine ruck size and has the all-round game to make it in the AFL.

22. Toby Krasna (24)

Northern Knights/Vic Metro

MID, 181cm

National Championships: 3 games, 19.0 disposals, 3.3 marks, 1.0 goals

Krasna plays with freedom and flair as an outside midfielder, taking the ball off the line with a quick few steps and executing his decisions well. He's a slighter frame that gets moved around easily as an inside midfielder so will likely play peripheral positions to begin his career.

23. Noah Williams (22)

Geelong Falcons/Vic Country

MID, 177cm

National Championships: 4 games, 15.5 disposals, 4.0 marks, 5.8 tackles

Williams is a hard-nosed inside midfielder that applies himself with courage defensively. He tackles hard and throws his body in harm's way to impact at stoppages. He's also shown the ability to defend well inside his own D50 and offers some run and dash off halfback which is where he likely begins his career.

24. Harvie Cooke (23)

Northern Knights/Vic Metro

MID/FWD, 176cm

National Championships: 4 games, 17.5 disposals, 7.0 marks, 1.0 goals

Cooke enjoyed a magnificent season as the Morrish Medallist in the Talent League and an undefeated Vic Metro campaign. He was a strong-bodied midfielder for the Knights then showed some aerial ability as a half forward for Metro. He likely ends up splitting time forward and through the engine room where his smarts can be utilised.

25. George Dimer (31)

Sandringham Dragons/Vic Metro

FWD, 173cm

National Championships: 3 games, 16.0 disposals, 5.7 marks, 1.0 goals

Dimer has a lot of tricks to his game. The small forward crumbs packs beautifully and has the burst to get himself out of trouble, but is also super creative to set up teammates in the forward half. He positions himself in dangerous areas consistently, smartly using his body to protect drop zones and create chances for himself and others.

26. Lochie Burrows (29)

Sandringham Dragons/Vic Metro'

181cm, DEF/MID

National Championships: 4 games, 13.0 disposals, 4.8 marks, 1.8 tackles

Burrows is firmly in the mix as a first round pick. He's an ultra-competitive utility, able to provide bounce off halfback, contested gruntwork through the middle or a smaller marking option up forward. His best traits may come as a defensive midfielder with running power and physicality, though he doesn't thrive in any one role.

27. Harrison Chapman (26)

Eastern Ranges/Vic Metro

MID, 190cm

National Championships: 3 games, 18.7 disposals, 4.7 marks, 2.0 tackles

There's serious upside to Chapman with his size, running power and skill. He's a natural outside midfielder and often gets bodied away from the ball in the contest, but in space he can execute and become a metres gained player. He needs to build size to his frame and improve his intensity at times to make it.

28. Marlon Neocleous (25)

Gippsland Power/Vic Country

FWD/MID, 168cm

National Championships: 2 games, 16.0 disposals, 5.0 marks, 0.5 goals

Neocleous is a crafty small forward that loves to get amongst the goals and has the celebrations to match. He also doesn't possess the pace to separate from the best lockdown defenders which limits his upside. Neocleous loves to get up the ground and is incisive with his ball use which could be a tool for him to get involved at the next level.

29. Lachie Hicks (35)

Western Jets/Vic Metro

MID, 183cm

National Championships: 16.8 disposals, 4.5 marks, 2.0 tackles

A wildcard pick through the middle rounds. Hicks is an elite athlete that could explode in the right environment. He blends strong endurance with a terrific speed and evasiveness combination that makes him hard to tackle through the contest and a nightmare in open space. Hicks racks up the ball consistently but has issues with his ball use that need to be rounded out.

30. George Gale (33)

Claremont/Western Australia

MID, 190cm

National Championships: 4 games, 27.8 disposals, 5.2 marks, 2.8 tackles

Gale's strong running and mature body should see him play early and often next year. He can play inside and outside of the contest with good discipline and defensive intent, and offered strong contributions for Claremont in his WAFL stints to end the season.

31. Jake Soutar (-)

East Perth

DEF, 190cm

The 20-year-old Soutar may be the best interceptor in the draft crop. He's a natural reader of the play and has sure hands when chopping off attacking forays, plus possesses a big boot and hits the ground running to kickstart transition. Soutar is the best mature-ager available this year.

32. Wil Antrobus (-)

Dandenong Stingrays/Vic Country

DEF, 182cm

National Championships: 4 games, 16.3 disposals, 3.0 marks, 2.8 tackles

There's a clearly defined role for Antrobus at the next level. He's a designated kicker with a sweet left boot, gaining chunks at a time with penetration from deep in defence. The small defender is limited by his size in defensive contests but plays with an edge and offers good run off halfback.

33. Gabe Patterson (27)

Glenelg/South Australia

FWD, 184cm

National Championships: 4 games, 13.0 disposals, 2.5 tackles, 1.0 goals

Patterson plays hard and tough footy in the forward half. He digs in defensively and scraps for loose balls, then grits the teeth and chases with vigour defensively. Offensively he straight lines the ball and plays through contact with power, plus can finish off his chances in front of goal.

34. Jackson Phillips (36)

Dandenong Stingrays/Vic Country

182cm, MID

National Championships: 4 games, 16.2 disposals, 3.8 marks, 3.2 tackles

A natural wingman at the next level, Phillips runs hard both ways and uses it safely off his preferred left. He doesn't try to do too much with the ball or take on the risky options, and can fade out of games in those peripheral roles, but projects to have a good floor at the next level with his running and skills.

35. Billy Wigmore (-)

Western Jets/Vic Country

DEF, 189cm

National Championships: 4 games, 17.0 disposals, 5.8 marks, 1.8 tackles

Wigmore is an elite interceptor. He reads the play, peels off and has strong hands in the air. There are worries in how it translates to the next level at his size, but there's no doubting he could have a Tom Stewart-like impact if it all comes together.

36. Keenan Boi (Hawthorn NGA) (28)

Gippsland Power/Vic Country

180cm, FWD

National Championships: 3 games, 13.3 disposals, 4.7 marks, 1.0 goals

Boi makes something happen whenever he's around the footy. He's tough and powerful plus applies some of the best defensive pressure you'll see in the draft class. With the ball in hand he makes quick, easy decisions and executes well. There's every chance Boi becomes a reliable pressure forward that can link play up the ground.

37. Albert MacGowan (30)

Sandringham Dragons/Vic Metro

187cm, MID

National Championships: 4 games, 22.8 disposals, 6.2 marks, 1.0 tackles

MacGowan finished the year on a tear. He was Sandringham's best player through finals and took out the 2km time trial. There's reason to believe he will become a good winger at the next level; MacGowan is fantastic in the air at his size, runs all day and plays a disciplined role for his side.

38. Sam Devers (previously: 32)

Eastern Ranges/Vic Metro

DEF, 189cm

National Championships: 2 games, 12.0 disposals, 2.5 marks, 1.0 tackles

Devers offers an excellent athletic profile but missed a significant chunk of his top-age year. At his best he can put speed on the ball out of defence, though he's also shown flashes further up the field with his burst. It's likely Devers settles into a lockdown role out of defence where he can use his athleticism to impact.

39. Marcus Prasad (37)

Dandenong Stingrays

167cm, FWD/MID

Talent League: 10 games, 18.6 disposals, 4.8 tackles, 2.0 goals

Prasad has some special traits at his diminutive size. He rarely fumbles below his knees and can draw free kicks with his quickness through contests. He lacks penetration on his preferred left and will struggle to push further up the field at his size, but as a genuine small forward there's a lot to work with.

40. Archie Elliott (-)

GWV Rebels/Vic Country

FWD, 182cm

National Championships: 4 games, 6.0 disposals, 3.5 marks, 1.8 goals

Elliott kept on kicking goals late in the year. He's a good size to impact aerially and when the ball hits the deck, and plays with real confidence around the ball. Elliott can get out the back of his opponent quickly and effectively by reading the contest and has kicked some brilliant goals from open play this year.

41. Blake Justice (Essendon NGA) (-)

Calder Cannons/Vic Metro

MID, 191cm

National Championships: 2 games, 12.0 disposals, 4.5 marks, 0.5 goals

Justice is a unique prospect - he ran fastest across state and national combines for the 20m sprint and his blend of acceleration at his height gives him ample opportunity to win his own ball and explode from contest. Around the ground he gets to a lot of contests and has quick hands but also fades out of games and doesn't have the forward nous required to play multiple roles for a team.

42. Harvey Spawton-Guy (-)

West Perth/Western Australia

FWD/DEF, 196cm

National Championships: 4 games, 8.5 disposals, 4.0 marks, 1.5 goals

Spawton-Guy is a competitor. He fights hard for position in marking contests and invariably brings the ball to ground where he butters up with a physical presence. He's also shown some chops as a resolute key defender and that flexibility appeals to clubs.

43. Mason McGroder (Swans Academy) (-)

Swans Academy/Allies

DEF, 194cm

National Championships: 1 game, 12.0 disposals, 4.0 marks

He's been well-documented since blitzing the national combine, but McGroder is one of the best athletes to enter the AFL system in some time. He turned his back on a pursuit of long jumping after winning silver at the U20 world championships in Oregon this year. He straight lines the ball with blistering pace off halfback and can play way bigger than his frame suggests with an enormous leap. There are significant challenges around his ball skills and reading of the play developing in front of him, but Sydney is a good place for him to develop at the lower levels.

44. Darcy Szerszyn (-)

Dandenong Stingrays/Vic Country

DEF, 190cm

National Championships: 4 games, 16.8 disposals, 5.0 marks, 1.0 tackles

Szerszyn is a great size for a defender, able to play on smalls and talls with quickness and physicality. He missed significant chunks of the season through injury but showed a lot of promise coming into his top-age campaign that he could make good on in a professional environment.

45. Jack Slattery (-)

Woodville-West Torrens/South Australia

FWD, 191cm

National Championships: 4 games 11.3 disposals, 4.3 marks, 4.0 goals

Slattery was a standout at the National Championships as a rare over-ager. He took advantage of opportunities with an excellent set shot and, while not being a genuine key forward height, used his frame well to protect the ball drop in marking contests and get on the move to find the dangerous space. He should get a shot on an AFL list to continue his rapid development.

46. Xavier Ladbrook (38)

Gippsland Power/Vic Country

DEF, 201cm

National Championships: 4 games, 11.5 disposals, 5.5 marks, 0.8 goals

Rated as the fourth key defender in the draft class, Ladbrook is a good runner that has spent time up on a wing or roaming forward as well. He plays within himself with safe ball use and doesn't have the intercepting prowess of Power teammate Snell but offers interesting traits for teams to invest in with the running power at his height. He will need to build size to play down back in the future.

47. Archie Van Dyk (-)

South Adelaide/South Australia

MID, 191cm

National Championships: 1 game, 21.0 disposals, 3.0 marks, 1.0 tackle

Van Dyk excelled against the bigger bodies in the SANFL Reserves and will be at home with the physicality of senior football. He's a tough in-and-under midfielder with great hands under pressure, but limited scope to play outside of the midfield.

48. Benji Van Rooyen (39)

Claremont/Western Australia

203cm, RUC

National Championships: 4 games, 14.0 disposals, 4.0 marks, 20.5 hitouts

Van Rooyen was the best performing ruck at the National Championships. Working against him is the time he may take to develop his conditioning and aerial presence on an AFL list. He's a competitor that, while lacking brother Jacob's athleticism, has safe hands and a selflessness that works alongside his midfielders.

49. Cody Templeton (40)

Gippsland Power/Vic Country

FWD, 180cm

National Championships: 3 games, 10.3 disposals, 1.3 tackles, 1.7 goals

Templeton saved his best performance for last, booting five goals in the Talent League grand final. The powerful forward can be a difficult matchup; always on the move and able to separate quickly, he's been hot and cold all season and the inconsistency has hurt his stock. His draft range may not begin much earlier than this point but Templeton should get an opportunity on an AFL list.

50. Brady Wright (-)

Werribee VFL

FWD, 195cm

Another mature-ager who produced big numbers in the VFL. Wright is a plug-and-play option up forward with great spatial awareness in marking contests and a reliable set shot routine. He stepped up this year to match the physicality of key defenders and will get his shot on an AFL list.

stories.headline: Patrick and Brittany Mahomes announce baby No. 4 on NFL trade deadline day
stories.summary: The couple shared the news on a busy trade deadline day that also brought receiver Josh Downs to Kansas City.
stories.body:
Trade deadline day in the NFL brought additions on and off the field for Patrick Mahomes.

The Kansas City Chiefs quarterback and his wife, Brittany, announced Tuesday in a joint Instagram post that they are expecting their fourth child. The couple shared beachside family photos featuring their three children in the announcement.

"Another blessing from God ... & then there were 6," they wrote with accompanying emojis.

The announcement means another sibling for daughters Sterling Skye, 5, and Golden Raye, 1, and son Patrick "Bronze" Lavon Mahomes III, 3. Patrick and Brittany were high school sweethearts in Texas before getting married in Hawaii in March 2022.

The family announcement capped a busy day for Mahomes, who also welcomed a new teammate in Kansas City. Earlier Tuesday, the Chiefs acquired wide receiver Josh Downs and a 2027 seventh-round pick from the Indianapolis Colts for fourth- and fifth-round selections.

stories.headline: MrBeast, meet Haaland: Man City star puts YouTuber through soccer gauntlet
stories.summary: Manchester City star Erling Haaland has collaborated with popular YouTuber "MrBeast" in a series of various soccer challenges.
stories.body:
Manchester City star Erling Haaland is known for his extraordinary feats on a soccer pitch, but this time he decided to put that to the test by allowing famous YouTube star James Stephen "Jimmy" Donaldson -- better known as "MrBeast" -- to participate in a series of intense soccer challenges known as the "Erling Haaland Gauntlet" at the club's training ground.

Posted on the Norway international's YouTube channel, which currently has over four million subscribers, Haaland put MrBeast -- alongside his two friends Tareq Salameh and Nolan Hansen -- through several soccer challenges to test their skill, strength and endurance.

The challenges consisted of sprints, wall sits, headers and a crossbar challenge, in which the winner would get a "Haaland Hammer," and the loser would have to go into goal and get hit by free shots from the penalty spot.

In the end, it was Salameh who ended up winning the "Haaland Hammer" after finishing first amongst the three, and it was MrBeast who had the misfortune of getting hit with shots from his two friends and, of course, Haaland.

It's safe to say that the most-subscribed YouTuber with over 526 million -- who's known for his extraordinary challenges -- probably doesn't have what it takes to cut it as a professional soccer player.

While it is currently the international break, that doesn't mean Haaland will relax while there are no matches for Manchester City. The 26-year-old was called up to play for his national team this month against Wales and Denmark in the final matches of their UEFA Nations League A campaign.

They are currently last in Group 4, as they look to qualify for the quarterfinal of the competition.

stories.headline: CF Montréal owner Joey Saputo announces club is up for sale
stories.summary: CF Montréal owner Joey Saputo announced Monday that he has initiated the sale of the MLS club his family founded in 1992.
stories.body:
CF Montréal owner Joey Saputo announced he will initiate the process of sale for the Major League Soccer club.

"After more than three decades of commitment, we believe this is the appropriate time to begin the process of identifying new ownership for CF Montréal," Saputo said on Monday. "This club has been a central part of our lives."

The Saputo family first founded the Montreal Impact in 1992 before the club became the Canadian MLS team CF Montréal in 2012.

"We have dedicated significant time, energy and resources to building it, and we are proud of what CF Montréal has become. I would also like to thank the fans, whose passion and loyalty have been at the heart of this club," Saputo said.

"We believe this is the right time to welcome a new ownership group with the resources, vision and commitment to build on the strong foundation we have established and carry forward the club's proud legacy."

Montréal concluded the 2026 regular season in last place of the Eastern Conference table with 26 points and just six wins in 34 games. The team fired head coach Marco Donadel in April after a slow start to the season, letting go of Montreal's 11th manager in 14 seasons.

Saputo confirmed the team will continue to be operational until a sale is confirmed.

Saputo added he prefers the team be sold to a local buyer, but cannot control if the team relocates to another market.

"If the club doesn't find a local buyer and I get an offer where the club needs to be relocated, then I have no choice. That is the decision I will take," he said. "Our clear preference is to find a buyer who shares our commitment to Montréal and who will ensure the club remains in the city."

The Saputo family has retained BMO Capital Markets as lead financial advisor and National Bank Financial as co-advisor to manage the sale process and identify potential buyers.

The club announced that day-to-day operations will continue as usual throughout the selling period.

stories.headline: Toto Wolff: Mercedes face fierce 2027 battle after winning constructors' title
stories.summary: Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff has played down the suggestion his team is about to embark on another period of dominance in Formula 1, and believes the battle for the 2027 title has already started.
stories.body:
Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff has played down the suggestion his team is about to embark on another period of dominance in Formula 1, and believes the battle for the 2027 title has already started.

They sealed the constructors' championship with three races of the season remaining at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix on Sunday, just one week after Kimi Antonelli secured the drivers' championship in Mexico City.

The German manufacturer stole a march on its rivals at the start of the year following the introduction of new engine regulations and has continued to be competitive throughout the season.

But after winning just one race in the last five, Wolff believes rival teams Red Bull, McLaren and Ferrari are in a position to pose a serious threat for the title in 2027.

"Look at the last few races, we haven't won," Wolff said. "And today at the beginning of the race, Kimi was just storming away, it looked like this could be ours, but the competition has been getting tougher, between Ferrari, McLaren, Red Bull and ourselves.

"It's four teams that can win races and will be challenging for a world championship. And I have no doubt that it's going to be very difficult for us next year.

"So for me, the 2027 season has started now. It is about learning in the three last races.

"What is it we can optimise? What didn't we spot when we put the upgrade on the car? What is it we can learn from today, and attack these last three races full blast, whilst also making sure that we have the learning for next year's power unit and next year's car."

Wolff believes the sheer quality of the top teams on the grid means the era of runaway teams in new regulations cycles -- such as Mercedes from 2014 and Red Bull from 2022 -- is a thing of the past.

"It looks like the most competitive era that is about to start, because the teams have become so professional in capability, in resource, that these kind of runaway seasons, I don't see them anymore, whether it's four in a row or eight in a row," he said. "And that is a completely new challenge.

"You can see how quickly it goes from being dominant and within a few races you realise that your upgrade doesn't work and you fall back and you're just third on the road. So it's great for the sport.

"I wish it was the era of Mercedes and me running away with another few titles, but I don't think it's the reality."

- Wet weather mastery by Norris, Verstappen makes Brazil F1's must-see race

- Mercedes completes the double with constructors' title at São Paulo Grand Prix

Wolff believes one of the keys to Mercedes' success remains its no-blame culture and its ability to empower its employees.

"We have stability certainly as a factor, but we have also many people that have joined us recently, and I think what I would like to choose as a word is safety. We are not a high-and-fire organisation.

"We provide a culture and an environment where you can thrive, where you are allowed to make mistakes, where you can speak up. And over the long term, I believe, if you want to be successful, not over a period of a few years, but over many decades, this is what you need to be able to kind of ingrain in the team. And we're trying that.

"It's not something you put on a PowerPoint. You have to live those standards in and out. These are the standards we are setting for ourselves.

"Sometimes we fail, but we look at the long-term vision. For me, soon is in ten years, and I need to set the team up for soon."

stories.headline: A timeline of how Donald Trump, Dana White forged friendship through the fights
stories.summary: Donald Trump and Dana White's friendship is on display cageside, on political stages and at the White House.
stories.body:
Editor's note: This story has been updated after originally being published in June 2026 before the UFC Freedom 250 event at the White House.

THE 28TH INSTALLMENT of the Ultimate Fighting Championship was a trial run. Though 36 states had banned the UFC, the New Jersey State Athletic Control Board allowed the then-owner, Semaphore Entertainment Group, to host its first sanctioned event on Nov. 17, 2000, at the Taj Mahal in Atlantic City, a hotel and casino owned by real estate mogul Donald Trump.

Fighter Randy Couture returned to the UFC for the first time since 1997 and recaptured his heavyweight championship against Kevin Randleman in the main event, but the most consequential appearance that night happened in the crowd of 5,000 fans.

Dana White attended, not as a UFC official but as the manager of fighter John Lewis. White was with friends Lorenzo Fertitta and Frank Fertitta III, brothers who were Las Vegas casino owners and trained in jiu-jitsu under Lewis. As they soaked in the atmosphere, they discussed all the things they could do when the Fertittas' company, Zuffa LLC, owned an MMA promotion.

Three months later, White returned to Atlantic City as UFC president at Trump's Taj Mahal for UFC 30.

That was a launching pad for the UFC and the beginning of a 25-year friendship between Trump and White that has led to Trump attending numerous UFC events, including four as a sitting president, and White introducing presidential candidate Trump at two Republican National Conventions.

"He is one of my very good friends," White told ESPN before the UFC held a fight card at the White House in June, adding that Trump is one of 10 friends in his small circle. "Like, you have a group of friends in your life that are, especially at my age, you've gone through all the s--- in your life and all this stuff. Me and this guy have been friends for 25 years and ... our relationship gets stronger every year."

On June 14, Trump's 80th birthday, their friendship reached a new landmark when the White House hosted UFC Freedom 250. Presidents have invited championship teams to visit the White House, hosted amateur games on the South Lawn and played tennis or basketball there themselves. But the UFC card was unprecedented -- a live professional sporting event staged on the White House grounds. ESPN combed through archival content from dozens of outlets to present the many ways two careers have crossed, creating a path for UFC fighters to walk into the Octagon on the South Lawn of the White House.

The timeline continues into the fall, with Trump inviting White to join his administration as press secretary. Or not.

• Jan. 11, 2001: Zuffa LLC purchases the UFC for $2 million and appoints White as the promotion's president. After having trouble landing a venue to host the UFC's two upcoming events, Zuffa makes a deal with Trump to host UFC 30 and UFC 31 back at the Taj Mahal in Atlantic City.

In all the years since, White has repeatedly expressed appreciation for Trump welcoming his company, saying the casino owner's involvement legitimized the UFC. "None of the venues wanted this," White told CBS's "60 Minutes" in 2025. "They didn't believe in it, they didn't like it, and they were worried about the type of crowd that would show up for this type of event."

After Trump stepped up, White remembered the time this way: "When the Trump brand was here [White holds his hand high overhead] and the UFC brand was down there [holding his hand near the floor], he saw it and said, 'I'd love to have it at my casino.'"

However, Trump's casino business faced severe financial problems at the time. According to PBS's "Frontline," his Atlantic City operation reported a net loss of $133.8 million for the 1999 fiscal year. The umbrella company holding the casinos filed for bankruptcy twice within the following decade.

• Feb. 23, 2001: The first event under Zuffa ownership, UFC 30, is at the Taj Mahal. In the main event, Tito Ortiz successfully defends his light heavyweight championship by slamming Evan Tanner unconscious in 30 seconds. White later said Trump was in attendance all night long at UFC 30 and UFC 31, also at the Taj Mahal, though ESPN could not find visual evidence of it, and the account has been disputed by multiple former UFC employees.

• June 29, 2001: The promotion's next fight card is at 20,000-seat Continental Airlines Arena, the East Rutherford home of the New Jersey Nets and Devils. For the first time, photos and the broadcast show Trump cageside. The UFC then books its next two fight cards in Las Vegas, at Mandalay Bay Events Center and at MGM Grand Garden Arena. White reflected on Trump's early support of the UFC in a 2011 interview, saying, "The guy saw this thing coming, was into it and gave us our first shot, and you'll never hear me say anything bad about Trump."

• Feb. 28, 2003: UFC 41 is held at Atlantic City's Boardwalk Hall, which has nearly three times the seating capacity of the Taj Mahal. Heavyweight Tim Sylvia and lightweight BJ Penn successfully defend their titles. Trump Plaza serves as the corporate host for the event, and the Taj Mahal casino features $5 chips with the UFC headliners' faces on them.

• Oct. 22, 2004: The UFC is back at Boardwalk Hall for UFC 50. It is headlined by Ortiz against a short-notice opponent, but the event is best known for being the card on which Georges St-Pierre first fights for a UFC title. St-Pierre loses to Matt Hughes. Also in the building is a production crew for the soon-to-debut reality TV show "The Ultimate Fighter." When TUF aired months after "The Apprentice" made Trump a reality TV darling, the show launched White to stardom, as well. A USA Today story drew a comparison, saying TUF had cast White in the "Donald Trump role."

• June 5, 2008: Trump calls a news conference at Trump Tower in Manhattan to announce a partnership with a startup MMA promotion, Affliction Entertainment, a venture of the Affliction clothing brand. The new promotion's star is heavyweight Fedor Emelianenko, widely considered the best MMA fighter in the world.

The Affliction brand had a long sponsorship history with the UFC, but when word got out that this new fight promotion was about to launch, the UFC banned its fighters from wearing Affliction clothing. At the introductory news conference, Trump acknowledges the potential competition between the UFC and Affliction by raising a topic that exists to this day in MMA: fighter pay. "If there's only one organization," he says, "you can pay the fighters five dollars and they'll be happy to fight."

However, Trump is not critical of the UFC boss. "I have great respect for Dana White," he says. "Some of the people in the room may not like him. I like him and I think he's done a very good job."

• July 19, 2008: Affliction Entertainment holds its first MMA event at the Honda Center in Anaheim, California, cheekily named "Affliction: Banned." It is headlined by Emelianenko knocking out former UFC heavyweight champion Tim Sylvia in 36 seconds. Two other former UFC heavyweight champs, Andrei Arlovski and Josh Barnett, fight on a card filled with talent signed away from the UFC. Megadeth, interrupting an international tour of summer music festivals, performs during the $39.99 pay-per-view.

Trump is asked afterward whether he thinks Affliction will take over MMA from the UFC. "I think it probably will," he says. "All the fighters want to be with us. I think it probably will take over."

That same night, the UFC holds a hastily scheduled fight card on five weeks' notice, made available on basic cable outlet Spike TV. The main event features a rare non-PPV appearance by the UFC's best fighter, Anderson Silva. White refuses to call this scheduling move counterprogramming, saying simply he is "giving the fans what they want."

• July 24, 2009: Almost exactly a year after its first MMA event, Affliction Entertainment folds. The abrupt end comes after one of the headliners on the promotion's third scheduled fight card, Josh Barnett, fails a steroid screening. Hours after the cancellation of "Affliction: Trilogy," the company announces it no longer will promote fights and instead will return as a clothing sponsor for the UFC.

This development shows White's business vision. At the UFC postfight news conference following Silva's KO win a year earlier, on the same night as Affliction's debut card, White had downplayed Affliction's chances of success, saying, "I figure after tonight those guys will be out of business." Asked why, White added, "Because they spent a lot of money tonight. And I know more about this business than they do. When you spend a lot of money and you don't get that money back, you usually go out of business."

White never mentioned Trump's name in his criticism of Affliction.

• Aug. 18, 2011: The UFC announces a seven-year, $700 million broadcast deal with Fox. White later revealed that Trump sent him a copy of a New York Times writeup about the deal with a note written on it that says, "Congratulations, Dana. I always knew you were gonna do it."

• Nov. 15, 2015: Hours after Holly Holm knocks out Ronda Rousey in a huge upset at UFC 193, Trump posts on X (then known as Twitter): "Glad to see that @RondaRousey lost her championship fight last night. Was soundly beaten - not a nice person!" Months earlier, Rousey had said she was voting for Bernie Sanders and downplayed Trump to CNN: "I don't want a reality TV star to be running my country." Rousey does not respond to Trump's "not a nice person" comment. Years later, she revealed that White asked her in 2016 not to speak badly of Trump. She said she agreed "because I owe Dana my life."

• Dec. 11, 2015: For the first time publicly, White backs Trump's presidential campaign. "Donald will get my vote," White says in an interview with TMZ.

• July 11, 2016: Steven Cheung, the UFC's director of communications and public affairs, leaves the promotion to join Trump's political campaign. Cheung had managed messaging for the UFC and its outspoken CEO since 2013. "When you're in communications, and you have a Dana White-type person, I think he would have learned a lot from that," UFC vice president of regulatory affairs Marc Ratner told NOTUS. "And that may have helped him there with the president."

• July 19, 2016: White speaks at the Republican National Convention in Cleveland, Ohio. The UFC CEO begins his address with, "What's up, GOP? ... I'm sure most of you are wondering, 'What are you doing here?'" He draws applause when he addresses why he supports Trump. "Let me tell you something: I've been in the fight business my whole life; I know fighters," White says. "Ladies and gentlemen, Donald Trump is a fighter, and I know he will fight for this country."

• Nov. 8, 2016: White and his wife, Anne, celebrate their 20th wedding anniversary in New York City and watch election night results from their hotel. When Trump is announced the winner, his son-in-law Jared Kushner calls White to invite him to Trump's victory party at the New York Hilton Midtown. White told reporters that Trump had planned to commemorate his victory at UFC 205 inside Madison Square Garden four days after getting elected. Ultimately, Trump did not attend the fights. "I don't think Donald really realized what his duties were going to be had he won," White said.

• July 11, 2017: At a prefight news conference for an upcoming Floyd Mayweather vs. Conor McGregor boxing match the UFC is promoting, White says the White House had reached out about securing tickets for the president, but ultimately Trump decided not to attend. "[Trump] feels like he'll ruin events," White says. "Secret Service is going to have to go through the place, shut down streets and create crazy traffic."

• Aug. 2, 2018: Trump hosts White and then-UFC fighter Colby Covington at the White House. In the wake of Covington's interim welterweight championship victory over Rafael dos Anjos in June, Covington and White visit the president to celebrate Covington's victory and shoot video for an upcoming UFC documentary.

• Nov. 14, 2018: UFC Fight Pass releases a mini-documentary online called "Combatant in Chief: the Story of Donald Trump's History in Combat Sports" that details White and Trump's long friendship. In a trailer for the film, which has since been removed from the UFC's channels, Trump says, "Well, there is a fighter's mentality -- whether you're in the UFC or whether or not you're president. People like Dana White have that and they have it in spades."

• Nov. 2, 2019: Trump becomes the first sitting U.S. president to attend a UFC event. As he walks out alongside White to cageside at Madison Square Garden in New York for the main card of UFC 244, headlined by Jorge Masvidal vs. Nate Diaz in the first BMF title bout, Trump is greeted by a mix of cheers and boos -- a more favorable reception than earlier in the week when Trump appeared at a World Series game in Washington to a "Lock him up!" chant from the crowd.

At the postfight news conference, White expresses no concern for the mixed reception Trump received. "This is America. You can believe and do whatever you want. If you want to boo, you can boo." he says. "... I just felt like tonight we were gonna walk in and whatever happened happened. The guy told me as a friend he would come see the fights, and he did tonight. I appreciate him, and it was a big night for the sport."

• Feb. 20, 2020: White appears at a Trump rally in Colorado Springs, Colorado, and says he and Trump have gotten closer since Trump was elected president.

• May 9, 2020: Trump congratulates White and the UFC on being the first professional sports league to resume action during the COVID-19 pandemic. "Get the sports leagues back, let's play," Trump says in a video prerecorded outside the White House's Oval Office that airs on ESPN before UFC 249. "Do the social distancing and whatever you have to do, but we need sports. We want our sports back."

• July 10, 2021: Trump attends UFC 264 at T-Mobile Arena in Las Vegas. This is his first appearance at a UFC event since the end of his first presidential run. Although Trump is in attendance, he is not shown on the broadcast. After the event, White expresses frustration with his production crew. "We were getting ready to show him right between the co-main and main events," White says in an interview with TMZ. "Let me tell you what, massive f--- up by my production team. But, you know, it's live TV and these things happen."

• Dec. 29, 2021: White appears on "The Fight with Teddy Atlas" podcast and recounts his appearance for Trump at the 2016 Republican National Convention. He reveals that his decision to appear was not popular among his associates. "Everybody, and I mean f---ing everybody, told me not to do it," White says. "I'm like, 'Are you crazy, man?' Yeah, there's no f---ing way in hell I'm not doing that for him. Then, once I spoke, you know, our friendship went to a whole 'nother level."

• April 8, 2023: After nearly two years without appearing at a UFC fight card, Trump makes an unannounced appearance at UFC 287 at Kaseya Center in Miami four days after he pleaded not guilty in New York to 34 felony counts of falsifying business records related to a cover-up of an extramarital affair. He walks to his seat flanked by White and another of his friends, musician Kid Rock, whose "American Bad Ass" plays in the arena.
